title: The headland
hookLine: be like the headland the waves break on; it stands, and the water settles (Meditations 4.49)
carry: spray flies up and falls back

lines: A ROCKY POINT IN A STORM.
cards: Stand on a rocky point in a storm. Gray waves come one after another and hit the rock with a sound like a slammed door. Spray flies up and falls back.
The water slides away, foaming, and goes quiet in the cove behind the point. The rock hasn't moved. It hasn't fought.
It just stood there, and the sea calmed itself around it. Marcus Aurelius saw that picture and kept it.

teach.b: Book four, entry forty-nine, in George Long's 1862 translation: "Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it."
A promontory is a headland: high land running out into the sea.
Notice continually. The waves don't stop because the rock is steady. Marcus isn't promising a life without trouble; he expects the waves.
And the rock doesn't attack the sea or argue with it.

teach.h: IT STANDS, AND THE WATER SETTLES.
teach.b: By staying where it is, it gives the water nothing to push against, and the fury spends itself and falls quiet.
The angry customer, the relative on the phone, the news crashing in all morning: the headland doesn't break them. It just doesn't move.

teach.h: A WEEK OF WEIGHTS SET DOWN.
teach.b: Now look back at this week. Be good while I can: don't save the good for later. Time gained: stop monitoring others.
No credit: do good without an audience. The emerald: what's good is whole unpraised. Do less: only what's necessary.
Each one sets down a weight: later, comparison, credit, praise, busyness, urgency. What's left is something like a rock in the sea. Not hard.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often call up the headland of Meditations 4.49 in conflict, staying steady and letting another person's anger spend itself.

o: a lighthouse that warns ships away from the rocks
the highest cliff, where you can see far out to sea
a rock that stands firm while waves break and calm

p: a headland running into the sea

s: Marcus promises the waves will stop if you're steady
they break continually; the rock stands anyway.
in the image, the rock tames the water without attacking it
it stands firm, and the fury of the water calms around it.
Long's translation calls the headland a promontory
high land running out into the sea.

games.q: a relative calls and starts in on an old argument, louder and louder. what fits the headland?
o: stay steady, say little, and let it spend itself.
games.why: Marcus's headland neither fights nor flees: it stands, and the fury of the water calms around it.

practice: Sit like a headland: feet heavy, back tall, shoulders loose. Let one frustration from this week come in like a wave, notice the spray and the urge to push back, and don't move.
Breathe, and watch it slide away; if another comes, let it break too.

wordCard.voice: The headland. Marcus says be like the promontory the waves keep breaking on: it stands firm, and the water calms around it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'height, headland, cape': the rock Marcus tells himself to be like in 4.49.

carryVoice: Your line: spray flies up and falls back. The rock stays; the water settles. Day five hundred sixty, a week well spent.
